name: Konkani
family: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan (Southern zone, closest to Marathi)
variety: Goan Konkani, the standard written in Devanagari (based on the Antruzi dialect); Mangalorean and Christian Goan varieties differ in vowels and vocabulary
sources: Miranda, Rocky V. (2003). Konkani. In Cardona, George & Jain, Dhanesh (eds.), The Indo-Aryan Languages. London: Routledge.
Almeida, Matthew (1989). A Description of Konkani. Panaji: Thomas Stephens Konknni Kendr.
Katre, Sumitra Mangesh (1966). The Formation of Konkani. Poona: Deccan College.
Sardesai, Madhavi (1986). Some Aspects of Konkani Grammar. Dissertation, Deccan College, Pune.

Fadte, Swapnil; Vaz Fernandes, Edna; Karmali, Ramdas & Pawar, Jyoti D. (2022). Acoustic analysis of vowels in Konkani. ACM Transactions on Asian and Low-Resource Language Information Processing 21(5), 1-13.
Fadte, Swapnil; Vaz, Edna; Ojha, Atul Kr.; Karmali, Ramdas & Pawar, Jyoti D. (2023). Empirical analysis of oral and nasal vowels of Konkani. arXiv:2305.10122.

Esposito, Christina M.; Khan, Sameer ud Dowla & Hurst, Alex (2005). Breathy nasals and /Nh/ clusters in Bengali, Hindi, and Marathi. UCLA Working Papers in Phonetics 104, 82-106 (mentions the breathy nasals of Konkani).
Masica, Colin P. (1991). The Indo-Aryan Languages. Cambridge University Press.

vowel_formants.speaker: adult male (mean of 3 speakers of Goan Konkani from different regions, vowels in read sentences)
vowel_formants.source: Fadte, Vaz, Ojha, Karmali & Pawar 2023, Table 5
vowel_formants.notes: Oral /ɛ/ is left out: the printed table gives F1 331 Hz for it, identical to /i/ and evidently a copying error (F2 1749, F3 2450; the nasal counterpart has F1 556). The female columns of the same table contain several repeated cells and are not used.

contrasts: four-way laryngeal contrast in stops and affricates: voiceless unaspirated, voiceless aspirated, voiced, breathy voiced
alveolar affricates /ts tsʰ dz dzʱ/ versus palatal affricates /tʃ tʃʰ dʒ dʒʱ/, written with the same letters
plain versus breathy voiced (aspirated) sonorants: /m n ɳ l ɾ ʋ/ : /mʱ nʱ ɳʱ lʱ ɾʱ ʋʱ/
nine oral vowels, with /e/ : /ɛ/ and /o/ : /ɔ/ and two central vowels, none of these contrasts shown in the script
oral versus nasal vowels for all nine qualities; nasality carries grammatical meaning (/hɛ/ 'these' : /hɛ̃/ 'this, neuter')
no vowel length contrast in the Goan varieties
allophony: /ɖ/ is a flap [ɽ] except word-initially and after a consonant
many speakers replace word-initial aspirates by plain stops; the following vowel is shorter after an aspirate or fricative, which keeps the contrast
the higher central vowel appears as an allophone of /ə/ when the next syllable has /ɔ/ (/ɡəʋɔ/ 'bison')
vowels are longer in monosyllables than in longer words
/ɭ/ is a retroflex lateral flap; /ʋ/ varies between [ʋ] and [w]
the palatal series is alveolo-palatal ([tɕ dʑ ɕ])
/f/ occurs in Portuguese and English loans and as a variant of /pʰ/
syllable_structure: (C)(C)V(C); clusters mainly in Sanskrit and Portuguese loans
phonotactics: word-final vowels are common because gender and number endings are vowels, often nasalised (masculine -o, neuter -ẽ)
the inherent vowel is dropped word-finally after a single consonant, as in Marathi
the script does not distinguish /e/ from /ɛ/, /o/ from /ɔ/, or the two affricate series

stress.rule: No fixed stress rule is established; prominence is phrasal.

rhythm.notes: Class and final lengthening are assumptions from the areal pattern; no measurement could be verified.

length.notes: Vowel length is not phonemic in Goan Konkani; Almeida 1989 treats it as phonemic, which Fadte et al. reject. No duration figures for geminates could be verified.

intonation.declarative: presumably the areal pattern: a rise on each content word phrase and a final fall to low
intonation.wh_question: prominence on the wh-word, final fall
intonation.continuation: high right edge on non-final phrases
intonation.notes: No instrumental description of Konkani intonation is known to me; all entries are inferred from related languages and are of low confidence.

phonation: breathy voiced sonorants /mʱ nʱ ɳʱ lʱ ɾʱ ʋʱ/

problems: The translator source has no entry for Konkani, so the Devanagari letter classes (vowel sign, consonant) are never set up and every rule that tests them fails. After a consonant each vowel sign and the anusvara is spoken by its name: भारत comes out as [bʰəaːkaːrɾət], देव as [dəeːkaːrwə], कोंकणी as [kəoːkaːrŋkəɳikaːɾ], हांव as [həaːkaːrshɪɾʌwinduwə]. Only words without vowel signs (घर, जग, फळ) and listed words are read correctly, so the voice is unusable for ordinary text.
For the same reason the default stress rule (penultimate) and default settings apply instead of the Indic ones.
The phoneme table is a copy of the Hindi table with a few length changes: there is no central /ɨ/, and /ɛ ɔ/ exist only as the Hindi long vowels.
The rules give च, ज, झ the palatal phonemes only; the alveolar affricates /ts dz dzʱ/ are missing.
Breathy sonorants are sonorant plus [h]; breathy voiced stops are a voiced closure plus a voiceless aspiration sample.
good: the rule file covers nasal vowels, final vowel length and the retroflex lateral, although these rules are not reached at present
retroflex lateral and nasal phonemes exist

notes: The two central vowels are written /ɨ/ and /ə/ by Fadte et al. and Sardesai; Miranda writes /ə/ and /ʌ/, and other descriptions use a rounded mid central symbol for the higher one. Only the two diphthongs written in the script are listed; more vowel sequences occur. No VOT table could be verified. Aspirated /tsʰ/ is rare.
